newsitem.title: UK: Air Gabon sees growing ex-UK/W.Africa cargo loads.
newsitem.headline: Air Gabon sees growing ex-UK/W.Africa cargo loads.

text.p: Air Gabon will increase the percentage of its ex-Britain freight loads to West Africa to the detriment of volumes to South Africa during 1997, its UK cargo sales agent ANA Aviation Services said.

"During the last six months, about 75 percent of our ex-UK freight on Air Gabon has been flown to Johannesburg, with the remainder to West Africa. But during 1997, I see the ratio changing to 60-40 South Africa/West Africa," ANA Aviation director, Gil Harding told Reuters in an interview.

He added that this forecast was based on two reasons, the first of which was the increasing popularity of Air Gabon's regular Boeing 737 freighter services from Libreville down the West African coast to Port-Gentil (Gabon) and Pointe Noir (Congo).

"Secondly, Air Gabon substituted a passenger Boeing 767 for a 727 on flights from Libreville to Angola and other points along the West African coast in December. Like the 737 services, this gives us a palletised cargo connection from London," noted Harding.

The African carrier, which split from Air Afrique in the mid-1980s to become the national airline of Gabon, commenced operating a weekly London Gatwick-Libreville-Johanneseburg service in July 1996 with a Boeing 747 Combi, capable of carrying 30 tonnes of cargo.
"Since day one, through traffic to South Africa has boomed. Our rates have been very attractive and most flights have been full," Harding added.

"To Gabon and other parts of Africa, from Britain we are mainly carrying oil industry equipment, while to South Africa it is computer equipment and general cargo. We are getting much higher yields to West Africa because that market is dominated by Air France and Air Afrique, which have traditionally charged high rates," he said.
In contrast, he added, the UK-South Africa market suffers from over-capacity, which has forced cargo rates down over recent years.

Harding nevertheless forecast that his through UK-South Africa officlal rates would be increased from March 1 and said he will be visiting Libreville this week to discuss this matter with the carrier's board.
"What will probably happen is that the current fuel surcharge imposed on the rates will be incorporated into the published rate," he said.
Apart from London Gatwick, Air Gabon also uses its sole 747 Combi to operate twice-weekly Paris-Libreville flights and a weekly Paris-Rome-Libreville-Johannesburg service.
"There is no chance of us getting any more capacity at present from London because the airline just doesn't have the aircraft," he said.
